content_blocks.text: You are a coding agent working in a checked-out repository. Prefer incremental edits, keep behavior stable, and verify each migration step with the smallest useful test slice before broadening coverage.

I need to port a Python 2 codebase to Python 3, but I don't want a flag day rewrite. Please do it incrementally: inspect the current failures, use 2to3 where it helps, patch what 2to3 misses, and rerun tests after each step. The codebase has a parser layer, a config loader, a small CLI, and an old urllib2-based HTTP helper. The target runtime is Python 3.11.

I will keep the migration staged. First pass is discovery: run a narrow pytest slice to surface the first Python 3 blockers, then use 2to3 on the modules behind those failures, patch any semantic gaps manually, and only then widen the test scope. I expect the first breakpoints to be print statements, exception syntax, iteritems/xrange, ConfigParser, and urllib2.

Initial failures are syntax/import level, which is a good sign for an incremental port: parser and config loader can be upgraded without touching the CLI or networking modules yet.

Python 3 porting guidance focused on the constructs showing up in the failing modules.

- The Conservative Python 3 Porting Guide recommends running tests first, then converting one dependency island at a time rather than sweeping the whole tree.
- The Python 3 porting HOWTO maps `print` statements to the function form, old `except E, exc` syntax to `except E as exc`, `ConfigParser` to `configparser`, and dictionary view methods like `iteritems()` to `items()`.
- For long-lived file and text code, the docs emphasize making string boundaries explicit: text is `str`, wire/file bytes are `bytes`, and comparisons between them should be removed rather than coerced implicitly.

2to3 fixer notes relevant here.

- `print`, `except`, `xrange`, `raw_input`, `ConfigParser`, and `urllib2` are handled mechanically.
- `2to3` does not resolve semantic issues around bytes/text, csv newline handling, or code that depended on list-producing iterators.
- The fixer output should be reviewed rather than committed blindly.

The mechanical syntax issues are gone. Remaining failure is the expected Python 2 to Python 3 boundary issue: config values are arriving as bytes in one path and text in another.

This is the right place to pause and fix semantics before broadening scope. I will look up the Python 3 file/text handling guidance, normalize config values to `str` at the loader boundary, and rerun the same slice. If that passes we can move outward to the CLI and HTTP helper.

Please keep the behavior stable for callers. Returning text from the config loader is fine, but I do not want to silently change parser semantics. Also, if there is a temporary compatibility shim, keep it localized so we can delete it once the port settles.

Python 3 text model notes.

- `open()` in text mode returns `str`; binary mode returns `bytes`. Libraries should choose one boundary and normalize there instead of mixing both through the call graph.
- The csv docs call out `newline=""` when opening files so universal newline translation does not corrupt parsing.
- `io.TextIOBase` and `io.BytesIO` are useful test doubles when tightening text-vs-bytes assumptions.

Porting guide note on iterator semantics.

- `map`, `filter`, and dictionary view methods are lazy in Python 3. Code that indexed or reused them like lists needs an explicit `list(...)` conversion.
- This often surfaces after syntax fixes, so small test slices are recommended after each migration batch.

The first dependency island is clean. Next I will widen to the CLI and the HTTP helper, because they are likely to trip over `raw_input`, `urllib2`, `has_key`, and implicit bytes from network reads. I will use the same pattern: run a narrow test slice, convert only the implicated files, patch leftovers, and rerun before touching anything else.

That sequencing works. Please keep the command-line output stable if possible because a wrapper script scrapes it. The HTTP helper only needs to keep GET and POST behavior; we can ignore legacy proxy code for now if it is not covered by tests.

Standard-library migration notes for the next batch.

- `urllib2.Request` and `urllib2.urlopen` move under `urllib.request`; quoting and parse helpers live in `urllib.parse`; HTTP errors come from `urllib.error`.
- `raw_input()` becomes `input()`.
- `dict.has_key(k)` becomes `k in dict`.
- Network reads now return bytes and must be decoded explicitly when the caller expects text.

What 2to3 will and will not do here.

- It will rewrite `urllib2` imports and many basic call sites.
- It will not choose an application charset for response decoding or decide whether a CLI should read from stdin as text or bytes.
- Review any change around subprocesses, sockets, or command output because Python 3 is stricter about bytes.

The widened slice reached one more Python 2 artifact outside the original batch: `list.sort(cmp=...)` in the runner. This is a good example of why the staged approach is safer than a tree-wide edit.

At this point the port is almost complete for covered code. I am going to fix the remaining `cmp` usage with `functools.cmp_to_key`, check for any adjacent legacy imports in the runner module, and then run the full test suite under Python 3.11. If the suite is clean, the remaining work is cleanup rather than migration risk.

Runner-layer migration notes.

- Python 3 removed the `cmp=` argument from sorting APIs. The supported port is `key=functools.cmp_to_key(old_cmp)`.
- The `imp` module is deprecated in favor of `importlib`.
- When preserving command output, prefer asserting exact stdout in tests before and after these migrations so sort-order changes do not slip in accidentally.

Import-system migration note.

- `importlib.util.spec_from_file_location` and `module_from_spec` replace common `imp.load_source` usage.
- This is typically a mechanical cleanup once tests are already passing again.

The Python 3 port is functionally complete for covered code. `2to3` handled the syntactic bulk, but the real migration work was in explicit text-vs-bytes boundaries, replacing lazy iterator assumptions, preserving CLI output, and converting `cmp`/`imp`/`urllib2` patterns to their Python 3 equivalents. Verification stayed incremental at each step and ended with `60 passed` on Python 3.11. The only follow-up I would schedule is deleting the localized compatibility shim in `legacy/config.py` once all binary-style callers are gone.
